title: The Rain on the Footpath and the Right to Livelihood
hook: When monsoon bulldozers tore down roadside shelters in Bombay, the Supreme Court held that stripping away a person's livelihood deprives them of life itself.
laws: Constitution of India (Article 19(1)(e), Article 19(1)(g), Article 21, Article 32, Article 39(a), and Article 41)
Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888 (Section 3(w), Section 61, Section 289, Section 312, Section 313, and Section 314)

facts.label: Court
facts.value: Supreme Court of India (Five-Judge Constitution Bench)

facts.label: Triggering Action
facts.value: Announcement on July 13, 1981 to evict and deport Bombay pavement and slum dwellers, followed by monsoon demolitions on July 23, 1981

facts.label: Preliminary Objection
facts.value: Municipal counsel argued an August 4, 1981 High Court undertaking estopped the petitioners from asserting fundamental rights

facts.label: Outcome
facts.value: Right to livelihood recognized under Article 21; statutory eviction power upheld subject to fair hearing and a post-monsoon stay until October 31, 1985

summary: On July 13, 1981, the Maharashtra government announced that all pavement and slum dwellers in Bombay would be evicted and deported outside the city, and municipal crews demolished roadside shelters along the Western Express Highway and Tulsi Pipe Road on July 23, 1981. After an interim High Court petition ended with a written undertaking to vacate by October 15, 1981, pavement dwellers, civil liberties groups, and two journalists moved the Supreme Court under Article 32.

Before addressing the merits, the five-judge Constitution Bench rejected the municipal corporation's plea that the High Court undertaking barred the petitioners under the doctrine of estoppel. Ruling that there can be no estoppel against the Constitution, the court held that fundamental rights serve the larger public interest and cannot be bartered away by a litigant's concession.

On July 10, 1985, the Supreme Court unanimously declared that the right to life under Article 21 includes the right to livelihood, because no person can live without the means of living. Balancing urban safety against human dignity, the bench held that while no one has a right to encroach on public footpaths, Section 314 of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act requires fair notice and a hearing except in urgent cases, stayed evictions until October 31, 1985, and directed the state to honor its resettlement assurances.

judgment.outcome: Writ petitions disposed of with directions; right to livelihood affirmed under Article 21, Section 314 of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act upheld as discretionary rather than arbitrary, and evictions stayed until October 31, 1985.
points: There can be no estoppel or waiver against the Constitution; a citizen's concession in an earlier proceeding cannot bar them from enforcing fundamental rights.

The right to life under Article 21 encompasses the right to livelihood, read alongside the Directive Principles in Articles 39(a) and 41, so state action depriving a person of livelihood must follow fair, just, and reasonable procedure.

Footpaths and public streets are meant for pedestrian passage and safety, and destitute occupation out of helplessness is a civil trespass rather than criminal trespass under Section 441 of the Indian Penal Code.

Because Section 314 says the Municipal Commissioner 'may, without notice' remove encroachments, dispensing with notice is an exception for urgent dangers; ordinary removals require prior notice and an opportunity to be heard.

principles.name: No Estoppel Against Fundamental Rights
principles.meaning: An individual cannot waive or be estopped from asserting constitutional freedoms through an earlier concession or undertaking.
principles.inThisCase: Even though the petitioners had agreed in the High Court to vacate their huts by October 1981, the Supreme Court heard their Article 32 challenge on the merits.

principles.name: Right to Livelihood Within Right to Life
principles.meaning: The constitutional guarantee of life protects more than mere physical survival and includes the means of earning a living.
principles.inThisCase: Accepting empirical studies that pavement dwellers lived near their workplaces to survive, the bench held that arbitrary eviction threatens both livelihood and life.

principles.name: Fair Hearing and Natural Justice
principles.meaning: Public authorities must give affected persons notice and a fair opportunity to be heard before taking adverse action.
principles.inThisCase: The court read Section 314 of the municipal statute as discretionary so that prior notice and a hearing remain the rule except in emergencies.

takeaways: Fundamental rights cannot be waived or signed away under pressure.
State action that strips away a person's livelihood must follow fair and reasonable procedure under Article 21.
Even unauthorized occupants on public land are entitled to humane notice and a fair hearing before removal.

social.hook: Can a city tear down roadside shelters in the middle of the monsoon without giving notice?
social.script: Can a city tear down roadside shelters in the middle of the monsoon without giving notice? In July 1981, Bombay authorities demolished pavement huts and put migrant workers on buses out of town. When the dwellers moved the Supreme Court, the city pulled out an earlier High Court undertaking claiming they had already promised to leave. On July 10, 1985, a five-judge Constitution Bench ruled that fundamental rights can never be signed away by estoppel. It declared that the right to life under Article 21 includes the right to livelihood, required fair notice and a hearing before eviction, and stayed demolitions until after the monsoon. You be the judge. Full case notes are on the Courtroom Chronicles website.
